Indy's Clock Hands

CountingParadoxesAlgorithms
Game: Two hands are fixed at an angle; watch how often each lands on a red arc.
How to play: Throw the hands, or run many throws, and change the angle and the size of the red arc.

Look for the math

Both hands are thrown at the same time and locked at a fixed angle, yet each lands on red just as often as a single free hand.

Shifting a set on a circle

Picking a hand's direction is picking a uniformly random point on the circle. The second hand is the first point shifted by the fixed angle α. Shifting a set around a circle leaves its size unchanged — the cut where the circle is unfolded into an interval merely moves. So the chance of landing in the red set is the red fraction of the circle for both hands, whatever α is.

What the check found

The logic test samples many directions for several arc sizes and angles: both hit rates approach the red fraction. It also computes the exact joint probability by scanning the overlap of the red arc and its shift — a reminder that equal individual probabilities do not by themselves tell you how the two events depend on each other.

Set the angle to 0. Do the two hands now always agree?
